vtrmc-2007-01.title: Split the integrand
vtrmc-2007-01.body:
Write $\frac1{2+\tan\theta}=\frac{\cos\theta}{2\cos\theta+\sin\theta}$ and express the numerator through the denominator $D=2\cos\theta+\sin\theta$ and its derivative $D'=-2\sin\theta+\cos\theta$:
$$\cos\theta=\alpha(2\cos\theta+\sin\theta)+\beta(\cos\theta-2\sin\theta)\iff 2\alpha+\beta=1,\ \alpha-2\beta=0\iff\alpha=\tfrac25,\ \beta=\tfrac15.$$
Hence
$$\frac{1}{2+\tan\theta}=\frac25+\frac15\cdot\frac{D'(\theta)}{D(\theta)},$$
and since $D>0$ on $[0,\pi/2]$,
$$\int_0^x\frac{d\theta}{2+\tan\theta}=\frac{2x}5+\frac15\ln\frac{D(x)}{D(0)}=\frac{2x+\ln(2\cos x+\sin x)-\ln2}{5}\qquad(0\le x\le\tfrac\pi2).$$
(At $x=\frac\pi2$ the integrand extends continuously by $0$, and the formula gives $\frac{\pi-\ln2}5$.)

At $x=\frac\pi4$: $2\cos\frac\pi4+\sin\frac\pi4=\frac3{\sqrt2}$, so $\ln\frac{3/\sqrt2}{2}=\ln\frac3{2\sqrt2}=\frac12\ln\frac98$, and
$$\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{d\theta}{2+\tan\theta}=\frac{\pi/2+\frac12\ln(9/8)}{5}=\frac{\pi+\ln(9/8)}{10}.$$
∎

vtrmc-2007-01.title: Substitute $y=\tan\theta$ (official)
vtrmc-2007-01.body:
For $0\le x<\frac\pi2$ put $y=\tan\theta$, $d\theta=\frac{dy}{1+y^2}$:
$$I=\int\frac{dy}{(1+y^2)(2+y)}.$$
Partial fractions: $\frac5{(1+y^2)(2+y)}=\frac1{2+y}-\frac{y}{1+y^2}+\frac2{1+y^2}$ (check: $(1+y^2)-y(2+y)+2(2+y)=5$). So
$$5I=\ln(2+y)-\tfrac12\ln(1+y^2)+2\tan^{-1}y=\ln\frac{2+\tan\theta}{\sec\theta}+2\theta=\ln(2\cos\theta+\sin\theta)+2\theta.$$
Evaluating from $0$ to $x$ gives $\frac{2x+\ln(2\cos x+\sin x)-\ln2}5$ (and the case $x=\frac\pi2$ follows by continuity). With $x=\frac\pi4$,
$$\frac{\pi/2+\ln(3/\sqrt2)-\ln2}{5}=\frac{\pi+2\ln(3/\sqrt2)-2\ln2}{10}=\frac{\pi+\ln(9/8)}{10}.$$
∎

vtrmc-2007-02.title: Split each term
vtrmc-2007-02.body:
**(a)** $\dfrac{n}{(2n-1)!}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{(2n-1)+1}{(2n-1)!}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1{(2n-2)!}+\dfrac1{(2n-1)!}\right)$. Summing over $n\ge1$, the denominators $(2n-2)!$ and $(2n-1)!$ run through all $k!$, $k\ge0$, exactly once:
$$\sum_{n\ge1}\frac n{(2n-1)!}=\frac12\sum_{k\ge0}\frac1{k!}=\frac e2.$$
**(b)** $\dfrac{n}{(2n+1)!}=\dfrac12\cdot\dfrac{(2n+1)-1}{(2n+1)!}=\dfrac12\left(\dfrac1{(2n)!}-\dfrac1{(2n+1)!}\right)$. Summing over $n\ge1$ gives $\frac12\sum_{k\ge2}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}=\frac12\left(e^{-1}-1+1\right)=\frac1{2e}$.

(All series converge absolutely, so the rearrangements are legitimate.) **Answer:** (a) $\frac e2\approx1.35914$, (b) $\frac1{2e}\approx0.18394$.

vtrmc-2007-02.title: Sum and difference (official)
vtrmc-2007-02.body:
Let $A=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n}{(2n-1)!}=1+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n+1}{(2n+1)!}$ (shift $n\to n+1$) and $B=\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{n}{(2n+1)!}$. Then
$$A+B=1+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac{2n+1}{(2n+1)!}=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac1{(2n)!}=\frac{e+e^{-1}}2,$$
$$A-B=1+\sum_{n\ge1}\frac1{(2n+1)!}=\sum_{n\ge0}\frac1{(2n+1)!}=\frac{e-e^{-1}}2,$$
using $\cosh1$ and $\sinh1$ from the series of $e^{\pm1}$. Therefore $A=\frac e2$ and $B=\frac1{2e}$.

vtrmc-2007-03.title: Substitute $y=e^u$ (official)
vtrmc-2007-03.body:
Since $y(0)=1>0$, near $x=0$ the solution is positive and we may write $y=e^u$ with $u(0)=0$. Then $y'=u'e^u$ and the equation becomes $u'e^u=ue^u+e^ue^x$, i.e.
$$u'-u=e^x.$$
Multiplying by the integrating factor $e^{-x}$: $(ue^{-x})'=1$, so $ue^{-x}=x+C$, i.e. $u=xe^x+Ce^x$. The condition $u(0)=0$ gives $C=0$. Hence
$$y=e^{xe^x}.$$
Check: $\ln y=xe^x$, $y'=y(e^x+xe^x)=y\ln y+ye^x$, and $y(0)=e^0=1$. The right-hand side $y\ln y+ye^x$ is continuously differentiable in $y$ for $y>0$, so by uniqueness this is the solution (and it is defined and positive for all $x$). ∎

vtrmc-2007-03.title: Linearise via $u=\ln y$
vtrmc-2007-03.body:
Divide by $y>0$: $\frac{y'}{y}=\ln y+e^x$. With $u=\ln y$ this is $u'=u+e^x$, $u(0)=0$. One solution of the inhomogeneous equation is found by trying $u_p=axe^x$: $u_p'=ae^x+axe^x=u_p+ae^x$, so $a=1$. The general solution is $u=xe^x+Ce^x$, and $u(0)=0$ forces $C=0$. Hence $u=xe^x$ and
$$y=e^{xe^x}.$$
∎

vtrmc-2007-04.title: Ceva and angle bisectors (official)
vtrmc-2007-04.body:
By Ceva's theorem for the concurrent cevians $AP,BQ,CR$:
$$\frac{AR}{RB}\cdot\frac{BP}{PC}\cdot\frac{CQ}{QA}=1.$$
In triangle $BRC$, $RP$ bisects the angle at $R$, so by the angle bisector theorem $\frac{BP}{PC}=\frac{RB}{RC}$. Substituting,
$$\frac{AR}{RB}\cdot\frac{RB}{RC}\cdot\frac{CQ}{QA}=1\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\frac{AR}{RC}=\frac{AQ}{QC}.$$
In triangle $ARC$ the point $Q$ lies on side $AC$ and divides it in the ratio $AR:RC$; by the converse of the angle bisector theorem, $RQ$ bisects $\angle ARC$, i.e. $\angle ARQ=\angle QRC$.

Since $A,R,B$ are collinear, $\angle BRC+\angle CRA=180^\circ$. Ray $RC$ lies between rays $RP$ and $RQ$ (as $P\in BC$, $Q\in CA$), so
$$\angle PRQ=\angle PRC+\angle CRQ=\tfrac12\angle BRC+\tfrac12\angle CRA=90^\circ.$$
∎

vtrmc-2007-04.title: Converse view: the external bisector
vtrmc-2007-04.body:
Let $\ell$ be the line through $R$ perpendicular to $RP$; it is the external bisector of $\angle BRC$, i.e. the internal bisector of $\angle CRA$. Let $\ell$ meet $AC$ at $Q'$. By the angle bisector theorem in triangle $ARC$, $\frac{AQ'}{Q'C}=\frac{AR}{RC}$, and by the angle bisector theorem in $BRC$, $\frac{BP}{PC}=\frac{RB}{RC}$. Then
$$\frac{AR}{RB}\cdot\frac{BP}{PC}\cdot\frac{CQ'}{Q'A}=\frac{AR}{RB}\cdot\frac{RB}{RC}\cdot\frac{RC}{AR}=1,$$
so by the converse of Ceva's theorem $AP$, $BQ'$, $CR$ are concurrent, i.e. $BQ'$ passes through $X=AP\cap CR$. Hence $Q'$ is the intersection of line $BX$ with $AC$, which is $Q$. Therefore $RQ=\ell\perp RP$, i.e. $\angle PRQ=90^\circ$. ∎

vtrmc-2007-05.title: Conjugates (official)
vtrmc-2007-05.body:
Let
$$A=(2+\sqrt5)^{100}\left((1+\sqrt2)^{100}+(1+\sqrt2)^{-100}\right),\qquad B=(\sqrt5-2)^{100}\left((1+\sqrt2)^{100}+(1+\sqrt2)^{-100}\right),$$
$$C=(\sqrt5+2)^{100}+(\sqrt5-2)^{100},\qquad D=(\sqrt2+1)^{100}+(\sqrt2-1)^{100}.$$
By the binomial theorem the odd powers of $\sqrt5$ (resp. $\sqrt2$) cancel, so $C$ and $D$ are integers. Since $\sqrt2-1=(\sqrt2+1)^{-1}$, we have $(1+\sqrt2)^{100}+(1+\sqrt2)^{-100}=D$, and therefore
$$A+B=CD\in\mathbb Z.$$
Now $0<\sqrt5-2<\frac14$, $\sqrt2+1<2.5$ and $\sqrt2-1<1$, so
$$0<B<\left(\tfrac14\cdot2.5\right)^{100}+\left(\tfrac14\right)^{100}=\left(\tfrac58\right)^{100}+\left(\tfrac14\right)^{100}<10^{-4}.$$
Thus $A=N-B$ for an integer $N$ with $0<B<10^{-4}$, so $A=(N-1)+0.9999\ldots$ and the first four digits after the decimal point are $9$. (In fact $B\approx4\cdot10^{-22}$.)

**Answer: $9$.**

vtrmc-2007-06.title: A common null vector (official)
vtrmc-2007-06.body:
Suppose $\det(A^2+B^2)=0$. Since $A^2+B^2$ is a real matrix, there is a nonzero **real** column vector $u$ with $(A^2+B^2)u=0$. Then, using $A^T=A$, $B^T=B$,
$$0=u^T(A^2+B^2)u=(Au)^T(Au)+(Bu)^T(Bu)=\|Au\|^2+\|Bu\|^2.$$
As $Au$ and $Bu$ are real vectors, $Au=Bu=0$, and transposing, $u^TA=(Au)^T=0$ and $u^TB=0$. Hence
$$u^T(AX+BY)=(u^TA)X+(u^TB)Y=0,$$
so the nonzero row vector $u^T$ is in the left null space of $AX+BY$, and $\det(AX+BY)=0$, a contradiction. Therefore $\det(A^2+B^2)\neq0$. ∎

vtrmc-2007-06.title: Rank of a Gram matrix
vtrmc-2007-06.body:
Let $K=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\end{pmatrix}$, a real $n\times2n$ matrix. Then
$$AX+BY=K\begin{pmatrix}X\\Y\end{pmatrix},\qquad KK^T=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}A\\B\end{pmatrix}=A^2+B^2$$
(using $A^T=A$, $B^T=B$). For a real matrix, $\operatorname{rank}(KK^T)=\operatorname{rank}K$, because $KK^Tv=0\Rightarrow\|K^Tv\|^2=v^TKK^Tv=0\Rightarrow K^Tv=0$ for real $v$, so $KK^T$ and $K^T$ have the same null space. (The rank of a real matrix is the same over $\mathbb R$ and $\mathbb C$.)

If $\det(AX+BY)\ne0$, then $n=\operatorname{rank}(AX+BY)\le\operatorname{rank}K$, so $\operatorname{rank}(A^2+B^2)=\operatorname{rank}K=n$ and $\det(A^2+B^2)\ne0$. ∎

vtrmc-2007-07.title: Compare with $\sum\frac1{n(\ln n)^2}$ (official)
vtrmc-2007-07.body:
**The series converges.**

*Claim:* $n^{1/(\ln\ln n)^2}>(\ln n)^2$ for all large $n$. Taking logarithms, this says $\frac{\ln n}{(\ln\ln n)^2}>2\ln\ln n$, i.e. $\ln n>2(\ln\ln n)^3$. With $y=\ln n$ this is $y>2(\ln y)^3$, which holds for all large $y$ because $(\ln y)^3/y\to0$.

Hence for large $n$,
$$n^{-\left(1+\frac1{(\ln\ln n)^2}\right)}=\frac1n\cdot\frac1{n^{1/(\ln\ln n)^2}}<\frac1{n(\ln n)^2}.$$
The series $\sum\frac1{n(\ln n)^2}$ converges by the integral test: $\int_2^\infty\frac{dx}{x(\ln x)^2}=\left[-\frac1{\ln x}\right]_2^\infty=\frac1{\ln2}<\infty$. By comparison the given series converges.

**Answer: convergent.**

vtrmc-2007-07.title: Substitute $n=e^y$
vtrmc-2007-07.body:
Write $n=e^y$. The general term is $\frac1n\exp\left(-\frac{y}{(\ln y)^2}\right)$. The function $x\mapsto x^{-(1+(\ln\ln x)^{-2})}$ is eventually decreasing and positive, so by the integral test it suffices to look at
$$\int^\infty\frac{1}{x}\exp\left(-\frac{\ln x}{(\ln\ln x)^2}\right)dx=\int^\infty\exp\left(-\frac{y}{(\ln y)^2}\right)dy\qquad(x=e^y).$$
For large $y$, $\frac{y}{(\ln y)^2}\ge2\ln y$ (as $y\ge2(\ln y)^3$), so the integrand is at most $e^{-2\ln y}=y^{-2}$, which is integrable at $\infty$. So the integral and hence the series **converge**.
